title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
formal:
Do there exist universal constants \(C,B\ge1\), an integer \(b\ge1\), and one deterministic algorithm \(\mathcal A\) with the following property? For every integer pair \(N\ge2\), \(2\le s\le N\), given the pair in binary, \(\mathcal A\) outputs an explicitly listed rational matrix \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times N}\), with an integer row count \(m\ge1\), in at most \(BN^b\) Turing-machine steps, such that
\[m\le C s\ln(eN/s)\]
and
\[\forall x\in\mathbb R^N\text{ with }|\operatorname{supp}(x)|\le s,\qquad \frac23\|x\|_2^2\le\|Ax\|_2^2\le\frac43\|x\|_2^2?\]
The complete binary output must also have length at most \(BN^b\). The constants and the algorithm are common to every pair \((N,s)\).
definitions:
For \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\), set \(\operatorname{supp}(x)=\{j\in\{1,\ldots,N\}:x_j\ne0\}\) and \(\|x\|_2^2=\sum_{j=1}^N x_j^2\). A vector is \(s\)-sparse if its support has size at most \(s\), including the zero vector and all smaller supports. Matrix multiplication has its usual exact real meaning, \((Ax)_i=\sum_{j=1}^N A_{ij}x_j\), with rational entries viewed as reals. The displayed inequalities are the restricted isometry property of order \(s\) with distortion \(\delta=1/3\), for squared Euclidean norms. They must hold simultaneously for every support and every real choice of coefficients; no input distribution, typical-signal exception or probability of correctness is permitted. Columns need not be individually normalized to exactly one, provided the inequalities hold. The matrix is real, not complex.

Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(e=\exp(1)\), so \(\ln(eN/s)=1+\ln(N/s)\), which equals \(1\) when \(s=N\). The real-valued row upper bound is an inequality on the integer chosen by the algorithm; no additional rounding convention is needed. Constants \(C,B,b\) cannot depend on dimension, sparsity, a signal or a support. The case \(s=1\), excluded from the main domain, has the trivial single-row all-ones construction; at \(s=N\), the identity matrix satisfies the geometric requirement. No compression promise such as \(m<N\) is imposed in the dense regime.

Use one fixed deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite alphabet, no advice, randomness or oracle, and ordinary bit-level computation. Time is polynomial in the ambient dimension \(N\), not necessarily in the length of its binary input. In particular, the full matrix must be written; a succinct circuit for entries, an existential matrix description, or a real-number computation with unit-cost exact arithmetic is not the stated output model. All computation and output steps count toward the bound.

For a concrete self-delimiting binary encoding, let \(u(t)=1^k0\operatorname{bin}(t+1)\) for \(t\ge0\), where \(k\) is the length of the binary expansion of \(t+1\) without leading zeroes. The input is \(u(N)u(s)\) with no extra bits. The output is \(u(m)\) followed in row-major order by the \(mN\) rational entries. Encode \(p/q\) by one sign bit, \(u(|p|)\) and \(u(q)\), where \(p\in\mathbb Z\), \(q\ge1\), \(\gcd(|p|,q)=1\), and zero has numerator zero, denominator one and sign bit zero. The sign bit is zero for nonnegative numerators and one for negative numerators. No trailing bits are allowed. This represents every output entry exactly and counts its denominator and numerator lengths. Requiring reduced fractions is an encoding convention, since integer gcd computation is polynomial time. Invalid binary inputs can be rejected without changing the valid-input target; no asymptotic bound is required on malformed encodings.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a uniform deterministic construction exists, or an unconditional proof that it does not in the stated model. A positive answer supplies the finite algorithm and fixed constants and proves termination within the bit-time and output-length bounds, the row inequality and exact RIP for all permitted inputs and all real sparse vectors. The Lean proof must justify any rounding of other representations to the rational output actually printed. A negative answer must rule out every polynomial-time algorithm and choice of universal constants, not just one matrix family or verification method. A conditional lower bound alone is not an unconditional negative answer. Random existence, shorter random seeds, successful numerical recovery, statistical restricted isometry, a different norm, or an asymptotically larger row count does not suffice. This asks whether an algorithm meets the specified exact distortion guarantee; the numerical-target tolerance of 1/100 does not enlarge that guarantee.
why: A central gap between random existence and efficient explicit construction, with direct consequences for uniform sparse recovery and for how pseudorandomness controls exponentially many spectral constraints.

importance.reason: An optimal derandomization problem connecting compressed sensing, pseudorandomness, additive combinatorics and explicit geometric constructions.

progress.text: Bourgain and coauthors give explicit RIP matrices beyond the coherence-based square-root bottleneck in a restricted parameter range.
Bandeira–Fickus–Mixon–Wong compare deterministic verification methods and formulate frame-based routes toward stronger constructions.
Rao obtains optimal row counts with fewer random bits; the December 2024 revision appeared in Information Processing Letters 189 (2025), article 106553.

Fickus–Lake’s revised and published frame results describe minimal dependencies in doubly transitive equiangular tight frames; their introduction still identifies optimal deterministic RIP construction as open.
A new finite-orthogonal-space construction gives coherence-based RIP guarantees for specified parameter families; it does not claim uniform optimal row counts.

status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No uniform deterministic polynomial-in-N bit-time construction with the stated rational output, fixed distortion and optimal row bound was found in the bounded primary-source review. Rao’s optimal-row result still uses randomness; the older explicit result and the August2026 orthogonal-space construction have restricted parameter guarantees. Coherence and statistical sparse-recovery results do not establish this all-vector RIP target. New preprint proofs were not independently certified.

context_blocks.text: Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The condition has an equivalent spectral formulation. For a set \(S\) of column indices, let \(A_S\) denote those columns. Every eigenvalue of the real symmetric Gram matrix \(A_S^{\mathsf T}A_S\) must lie in \([2/3,4/3]\) whenever \(1\le|S|\le s\). Thus the target controls every linear combination within every small column set, not only column lengths or pairwise inner products.

Restricted isometry of order \(2t\) implies that different \(t\)-sparse signals have different measurements, since their difference has at most \(2t\) nonzero entries. At distortion \(1/3<\sqrt2-1\), the recovery theorem recorded by Bandeira and coauthors also gives robust reconstruction through \(\ell_1\) minimization. The reconstruction problem and its additional sparsity parameter are consequences, not extra outputs required of this construction task.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain \(m=O(s \log (eN/s))\) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for \(s\ge 2\). Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

The standard existence benchmark is compatible with rational entries. Normalized Bernoulli matrices with a square number of rows \(m=t^2\) have entries \(\pm1/t\), and rounding a positive row target up to a square changes its size by at most a constant factor. Thus the rational representation requirement does not itself obstruct optimal-order existence. The remaining demand is one deterministic algorithm with the proved time bound.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence \(\mu\), the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most \((s- 1)\mu\). When \(\mu\) is about \(1/\sqrt{m}\), this argument certifies only s on the order of \(\sqrt{m}\). This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova give explicit matrices beyond the square-root bottleneck. Their Theorem 1 specifies a restricted relation between row count and column count, with sparsity slightly above the square root of the row count. This is a positive construction theorem in that regime, but does not give the required optimal row order uniformly over all ambient dimensions and sparsities.

Rao’s construction attains the optimal row order using \(O(s\log(N/s)\log s)\) random bits in the sparse parameter regime stated in the paper, with distortion fixed. Its guarantee remains probabilistic and still uses a seed whose length depends on sparsity and dimension. Reduced randomness is distinct from a deterministic rule whose single output is proved to satisfy RIP on every allowed input.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the \(m+1\) unit vertices of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}\) have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The parameter range matters. For \(s\) comparable to \(N\), the identity matrix is compatible with the requested row order. The problem also includes all intermediate sparse regimes and arbitrary integer dimensions, whereas many algebraic constructions only give particular dimension sequences or sparsity ranges. Statistical guarantees for typical signals and restricted isometries in \(\ell_1\) are different targets.

The August 2026 preprint by Moonchaisook, Kumam and Sriwongsa gives further deterministic incidence matrices from finite orthogonal spaces. Its guarantee uses \(\delta_s\le(s-1)\mu\), where \(\mu\) is the normalized column coherence, and evaluates particular geometric parameter families. It does not claim the uniform \(O(s\ln(eN/s))\)-row construction required here. Numerical recovery comparisons in that paper are separate from the all-vector RIP theorem.

An older milestone, posed by Strauss at Kanpur 2006 and formerly indexed as TCS-0987, asks for a deterministic polynomial-time construction of a matrix with \(N\) columns and at most \(C s(\log_2(N+2))^a\) rows for fixed constants \(C,a\), preserving every \(s\)-sparse Euclidean norm within a factor of two after normalization. A precise rational-output specialization asks \(\|x\|_2\le\|Mx\|_2\le2\|x\|_2\) for every such vector. This card's optimal-row target implies that milestone: for its matrix \(A\), the rational scaling \(M=(3/2)A\) gives \((3/2)\|x\|_2^2\le\|Mx\|_2^2\le3\|x\|_2^2\), and \(\ln(eN/s)\le1+\ln N\). The weaker milestone does not conversely establish the optimal row count. The source also asks about certification and fast multiplication of Fourier submatrices; those separate questions are not additional requirements of the present construction target.

sentences: A restricted-isometry matrix approximately preserves squared Euclidean norms of every vector with at most a specified number of nonzero coordinates.
The question asks for one deterministic algorithm producing an explicit rational matrix with \(O(s\ln(eN/s))\) rows and distortion \(1/3\).
Its bit running time and complete output length must be polynomial in the ambient dimension, with constants common to every dimension and sparsity.
A complete Lean proof must establish the algorithm, its resource bounds and the simultaneous guarantee for all real sparse vectors, or prove unconditional nonexistence in the fixed model.
Random optimal matrices, reduced random seeds and coherence-based constructions for restricted parameter families do not meet this uniform deterministic guarantee.

source_formulation.text: Retains the saved optimal deterministic RIP construction question motivated by Fickus–Lake and the cited construction literature. The fixed squared-norm distortion 1/3, all-input row bound C s ln(eN/s), real signal space and explicit rational output are the previously selected variant. The finite encoding and uniform Turing-machine convention make that target precise without replacing it by coherence, statistical recovery or a restricted parameter family.
